title: The thread of compassion
hookLine: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot and truth the twist (Asa di Var, ang 471)

lines: THE BOY NANAK AND THE THREAD.
A THREAD NOT MADE OF COTTON.
cards: The courtyard is full. Relatives have come from nearby villages, food is cooking, and the family priest has arrived for an important day: a boy's investiture with the sacred thread.
The boy is Nanak, still young, in Talwandi. The janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak written down generations later, tell what happened next.
As the priest prepared the thread, the boy asked: what is this thread for? Will it last? Then he described the thread he would actually wear, and it wasn't made of cotton at all.

teach.b: The janeu is a sacred thread that Hindu families in some communities give their sons in a coming-of-age ceremony, worn across the body from the shoulder.

For the families who keep it, it marks a second birth into learning and duty, and it's held with real reverence. The salok on ang 471, which Sikh tradition links to young Nanak's day, doesn't mock the thread.
It asks for a deeper one.
In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul. If you have it, priest, then put it on me.
Daiaa, compassion, is the raw cotton, the stuff everything else is spun from. Santokh, contentment, from the servants' pauri, is the thread itself, the long continuous strand.
Jat, restraint, self-control, is the knot that holds it together. And sat, truth, is the twist that gives a thread its strength. Untwisted fiber pulls apart in the hands; spinners know it.
Truth is what makes the whole thing hold. Notice the order. Compassion comes first, as the material; everything after is shaping it.
A person could carry contentment, restraint, even truth, but without compassion there's nothing to spin.

teach.h: TRUTH IS THE TWIST THAT HOLDS.
teach.b: Sikhs remember this story as an early sign of who Nanak would become: not someone who rejects people's rituals for the sake of it, but someone always asking what's inside them.
Tomorrow, what he said such a thread could survive.

how: Sikhs remember the janamsakhi story of young Nanak and the sacred thread, and hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var as a call to wear the inner thread of compassion.

o: a turban tied at a coming-of-age
a prayer string for counting names
a sacred thread worn across the body

games.q: the thread of the soul — tap the pairs.

s: the salok mocks the sacred thread
it asks for a deeper thread, of compassion, contentment, restraint and truth.
in the salok, compassion is the raw cotton
everything else is spun from it.
the janamsakhis were written by Guru Nanak himself
they are life-stories written down generations later.

games.q: you're the young Nanak, and the priest is ready to put the sacred thread on you. what do you do?
o: ask about a thread made of compassion, contentment, restraint and truth.
games.why: the janamsakhis say he asked what the thread was for, and described the thread of the soul: if you have it, put it on me.

practice: Hold a piece of string, or just your fingers, and touch it: compassion, the cotton; run along it: contentment, the thread. Tie a loose knot, restraint, and give it a gentle twist, truth. If you pray, say Waheguru as you hold it.

wordCard.voice: Janeu. The sacred thread. In Guru Nanak's salok, a thread of the soul: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: janeu, the sacred thread given in a Hindu coming-of-age ceremony.

carryVoice: Your line: compassion is the thread. Everything else is spun from it. Day five hundred fifty-four, done.
